opus-5.5.text:
I think the trajectory is pretty clear: problems with well-defined answers and fast, reliable verification are the ones AI will saturate first, and math and programming contests are exactly that kind of problem. A proof either checks or it doesn't; code either passes the test cases or it doesn't. That gives you a very clean reward signal for reinforcement learning, so the model can keep improving through trial and error, not just by imitating human data.

So my expectation is that, in the near term, top contest-level performance stops being a meaningful differentiator. Reaching gold-medal level on olympiad problems, or ranking near the top of competitive programming, goes from headline news to something people take for granted. We've already seen that curve move much faster than most people predicted a few years ago.

But I'd add two caveats. First, contests are a proxy. They're useful because they're hard and measurable, not because solving them is the end goal. Once models saturate them, the real question becomes whether that reasoning ability transfers to open-ended work: research math where nobody knows the answer, or large real-world software projects with ambiguous requirements and long horizons. That's much harder to verify, and that's where the next frontier is.

Second, the bottleneck shifts. When the model can solve the problem, the scarce thing is knowing which problems are worth solving and how to specify them well. So for people, I think the value moves from raw problem-solving speed toward taste, judgment, and the ability to define good questions. And for us building models, the challenge is constructing environments and reward signals for tasks that don't come with a clean answer key. That's where I think the most interesting progress will happen over the next few years.

r001.rationale: The response says AI will saturate math and programming-contest problems first and expects top contest-level performance to become routine in the near term.

fable-5.1.text:
I think math and competitive programming are going to be among the first domains to fall, and honestly, in a lot of ways they've already fallen. The reason is structural. These are problems where the answer can be verified. You either solved the problem or you didn't, your code either passes the tests or it doesn't. Once you have a clean reward signal like that, reinforcement learning becomes extraordinarily effective, because the model can generate a huge amount of its own training data by trying, failing, and learning from what works.

So when people ask me about the rate of improvement, I don't think about it in terms of "will models reach IMO gold" or "will they beat the top Codeforces players." Those are milestones, and we've seen them approached or crossed much faster than most people predicted even two years ago. The more interesting question is what happens after the benchmark saturates. And my view is that these contests stop being a measurement tool and start being a training ground. They become the gym, not the exam.

What I'd caution against is extrapolating too directly from this to everything else. Contest problems have a property that most real-world work doesn't: the problem is fully specified, the environment is closed, and feedback is instant and unambiguous. A lot of what makes real mathematics or real software engineering hard is that you don't know what the right question is, or the verification takes months, or the reward is extremely sparse. So I expect a widening gap for a while, where models look superhuman on anything with a verifier and much more uneven on open-ended tasks.

But I'd also say the lessons transfer more than skeptics think. When you train a model to do long chains of reasoning on hard math, it learns something general about how to hold a problem in mind, backtrack, and check its own work. That capability shows up in domains that look nothing like a contest. So I'd describe the current rate as this: on contests specifically, we're near the end of the story. On what those contests teach the model, we're near the beginning.

r001.rationale: The response says math and competitive programming are among the first domains to fall, notes that key milestones have been approached or crossed faster than expected, and describes contests as near the end of the story. This communicates that many contest problems will soon be solved at the current pace.

astra-6.text:
I expect AI to get very good at those problems quite quickly. Math competitions and programming contests have clear rules, and you can usually verify whether an answer is correct. That makes them especially well suited to improving models through reasoning and feedback.

But solving a contest problem is different from doing original research or building useful software. In a contest, someone has already formulated the question. In practice, deciding what problem matters and how to formulate it is often a large part of the work. So I’d expect progress on these benchmarks to be faster than progress on the full range of tasks mathematicians and programmers do.

r001.rationale: The response predicts AI will get very good at contest problems quickly, but does not clearly predict that many current problems will be fully solved.

sol-6.1.text:
I think math and programming contests are areas where we could see progress very quickly, because you can verify whether an answer is correct. That gives you a clear signal for training: the model can try different approaches, get feedback, and improve.

If the current pace continues, I would expect AI to solve increasingly difficult contest problems, including problems that challenge very strong human competitors. But I’d distinguish that from doing original research or building a large software system. A contest gives you a well-defined problem and a way to judge the result. In research and engineering, figuring out what problem to solve is often a big part of the work. So I expect contest performance to advance rapidly, while broader capabilities will still require additional breakthroughs.

r001.rationale: The response expects rapid progress on increasingly difficult contest problems if the pace continues, but does not clearly predict that many current problems will be fully solved soon.
